content:
Here are the mascots of all eight Ivy League schools:

## **Ivy League School Mascots**

| School | Mascot Name | Type |
|--------|-------------|------|
| **Harvard University** | John Harvard | Founder (Puritan clergyman) |
| **Yale University** | Handsome Dan | Bulldog |
| **Princeton University** | The Tiger | Tiger |
| **Columbia University** | Roar-ee the Lion | Lion |
| **University of Pennsylvania** | The Quaker | Quaker |
| **Brown University** | Bruno the Bear | Brown bear |
| **Dartmouth College** | Keggy the Keg | Anthropomorphic beer keg |
| **Cornell University** | Touchdown the Bear | Black bear |

---

### **Notable Details:**

**Harvard** - Unlike most universities, Harvard uses its namesake founder John Harvard as its mascot. Their athletic teams are known as the "Crimson" (their school color), making them unique among Ivy League schools for not having a traditional animal mascot.

**Yale** - Handsome Dan is the oldest living mascot in American college sports, with the tradition dating back to 1889. It's an actual live bulldog that has been passed down through generations (currently in its 19th iteration).

**Dartmouth** - Keggy the Keg is the most unique mascot - an anthropomorphic beer keg created in 2003 by students. It's technically unofficial but has become ingrained in Dartmouth culture and was ranked #1 Most Unique Mascot by Yahoo Sports in 2012. Dartmouth's athletic nickname is the "Big Green" (their school color).

**Cornell** - Touchdown the Bear has a rich history dating back to 1915, with four live bears serving as mascots over two decades. A statue was erected in 2015 to commemorate the mascot's 100-year legacy.

**Columbia** - Roar-ee the Lion was officially adopted in 1910 and renamed in 2005. The lion symbol dates back to the university's founding in 1754 under King George II.

**Penn** - The Quaker mascot honors the university's founder Benjamin Franklin and Pennsylvania's colonial history with William Penn (a Quaker).

**Princeton** - The Tigers have been their mascot since at least 1904, known for the "Bengal tiger" nickname.

**Handsome Dan** is a [bulldog](Bulldog "Bulldog") who serves as the [mascot](Mascot "Mascot") of [Yale University](Yale_University "Yale University")'s sports teams. In addition to a person wearing a [costume](Costume "Costume"), the position is filled by an actual bulldog, the honor (and the title "Handsome Dan") being transferred to another upon death or retirement.

## Handsome Dan I

Active 1889–1897 (retired to England).  


Handsome Dan was selected based on his ability to tolerate bands and children, negative reaction to the color [crimson](Crimson "Crimson") and to [tigers](Tigers "Tigers") (the symbols of rival schools <Harvard> and [Princeton](Princeton_University "Princeton University") respectively), bought by Yale student Andrew Barbey Graves,[[1]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tale-1) who cleaned up the dog and named him “Handsome Dan.” Soon, Dan followed Graves everywhere around campus, including sporting events.[[2]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-MascotAudition-2)[[3]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanI-3) The students quickly adopted Dan as the Yale mascot. After Graves graduated and returned to England, Dan stayed on campus with his master's brother, William Leon Graves.[[1]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tale-1) Before football and baseball games would begin, Handsome Dan founded a tradition and a dynasty by being led across the field. One newspaper reported: "He was a big white bulldog, with one of the greatest faces a dog of that breed (English) ever carried". This was not an exaggeration, as Handsome Dan was one of the finest specimens of his breed in America, and went on to win first prize at the [Westminster Dog Show](Westminster_Dog_Show "Westminster Dog Show") and at least thirty other first prize ribbons in the United States and Canada.[[4]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tim_Cohane_pp._72-73-4) According to the [Hartford Courant](Hartford_Courant "Hartford Courant"), "In personal appearance, he seemed like a cross between an alligator and a horned frog, and he was called handsome by the metaphysicians under the law of compensation. The title came to him, he never sought it. He was always taken to games on a leash, and the Harvard football team for years owed its continued existence to the fact that the rope held."[[3]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanI-3) The Philadelphia Press reported that "a favorite trick was to tell him to 'Speak to Harvard.' He would bark ferociously and work himself into physical contortions of rage never before dreamed of by a dog. Dan was peculiar to himself in one thing – he would never associate with anyone but students. Dan implanted himself more firmly in the hearts of Yale students than any mascot had ever done before."[[1]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-Tale-1)[[3]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanI-3) Handsome Dan crossed the Atlantic to join his old master in 1897 and died in 1898. Graves had Dan [stuffed](Taxidermy "Taxidermy") and returned him to be displayed at Yale in the old gymnasium. When it was torn down, Dan I was sent to the [Peabody Museum](Peabody_Museum_of_Natural_History "Peabody Museum of Natural History") for reconstruction. Handsome Dan I now is in a sealed glass case in one of the trophy rooms of Yale's [Payne Whitney Gymnasium](Payne_Whitney_Gymnasium "Payne Whitney Gymnasium"), where, according to Stanton Ford, "he is the perpetual guardian of the treasures which attest to generations of Yale athletic glory." Andrew Graves died of [tuberculosis](Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis") on February 18, 1948, in Westbury, Long Island.[[5]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-5)

## Handsome Dan II

Active 1933–1937 (died of a broken leg).  
After a 35-year interval, Handsome Dan II was purchased with pennies donated by the freshman class, and given to [coach](Coach_(sport) "Coach (sport)") [Ducky Pond](Ducky_Pond "Ducky Pond").[[6]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanII-6) Handsome Dan II was [dognapped](Dognapping "Dognapping") by Harvard students the day before the 1934 [Harvard-Yale football game](Harvard-Yale_football_games_(The_Game) "Harvard-Yale football games (The Game)"), and Yale students were alarmed at photographs of him happily seated at the foot of the statue of [John Harvard](John_Harvard_(clergyman) "John Harvard (clergyman)") in [Harvard Yard](Harvard_Yard "Harvard Yard"), having a snack.[[6]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanII-6) He died of a leg fracture received from a jump. Handsome Dan II now is in a sealed glass case in the Yale University Visitor's centre on Elm Street.

## Handsome Dan III

Active 1937–1938 (retired due to emotional instability).  
Handsome Dan III was a huge white dog who exhibited morbid [fear of crowds](Agoraphobia "Agoraphobia") and had to be retired.[[7]](Handsome_Dan#cite_note-HandsomeDanIII-7)

- Basketball Arena: Jadwin Gymnasium
- Ice Hockey Arena: Baker Rink
- Baseball Stadium: Bill Clarke Field
- Soccer Stadium: Roberts Stadium
- Lacrosse Stadium: Class of 1952 Stadium

The tiger mascot has deep historical roots. Historical references from the early 1900s indicate that Princeton was already known as having the "Bengal tiger" as its mascot by 1904, when Penn State's legendary Nittany Lion was created as a fictional rival that would "easily defeat the Princeton Bengal tiger."

The tiger mascot reflects the strength, courage, and spirit associated with the animal, making it a fitting symbol for Princeton's athletic teams. The black and orange colors have been synonymous with Princeton throughout its athletic history and are recognized nationwide in collegiate athletics.

**Roar-ee the Lion** is the current incarnation of the **Columbia Lion**, the official mascot of [Columbia University](Columbia_University "Columbia University") and the [Columbia Lions](Columbia_Lions "Columbia Lions"). Already a long established symbol of the university, it was first adopted as the university's mascot in 1910 under the name "Leo Columbiae", and was renamed Roar-ee the Lion in 2005. Throughout its history, the Lion has been represented by live specimens on several occasions, including the [1934 Rose Bowl](1934_Rose_Bowl "1934 Rose Bowl") and a 1963 football game against [Princeton](Princeton_University "Princeton University"). During the early 20th century, Matilda the Harlem Goat was an unofficial mascot for the university. [Barnard College](Barnard_College "Barnard College") possesses its own mascot, the Barnard Bear.

## History

### Proposal and adoption

The idea of having a lion as the mascot of Columbia was first proposed by George Brokaw Compton at the April 5, 1910 meeting of the alumni association. The lion had been a longstanding unofficial symbol of the university, having frequently been used as a design motif on the university's campus even before its adoption. It was possibly derived from the coat of arms of King [George II](George_II_of_Great_Britain "George II of Great Britain"), under whom the school was founded in 1754.[[1]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-1)[[2]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-:2-2)

Its adoption was not uncontroversial, however. As the Lion, which was named "Leo Columbiae", was chosen in connection with Columbia's other royal imagery, a product of [Columbia's colonial past](Colonial_colleges "Colonial colleges"), some considered it a sign of excessive conservatism and a symbol of "servility to British Royalty".[[3]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-3) The Eagle was floated as an alternative, in line with the university's patriotic renaming following American independence: "For Kings College, the Lion, but the Eagle for [Columbia](Columbia_(personification) "Columbia (personification)")".[[4]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-4) The Goat, specifically Matilda the Harlem Goat, was also proposed, allegedly as a joke.[[5]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-5) Nevertheless, Leo was approved by the Student Board on May 4, 1910.[[2]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-:2-2)[[6]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-6)

### Live mascots

The first live Lion mascot used by the university football team was a [German Shepherd](German_Shepherd "German Shepherd") named Chief, who was presented to the team in 1925 and used for a short period of time.[[7]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-7) On October 24, 1928, a freshman suggested in the *[Columbia Daily Spectator](Columbia_Daily_Spectator "Columbia Daily Spectator")* that the university acquire an actual lion to use at football games, claiming that lions "are not very expensive at wild animal dealers," and "would grow up well tamed, meek and mild" if purchased as cubs.[[8]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-8) Several days later, an alumnus offered to donate a live lion cub to the university to serve as its mascot, which football Coach Charley Crowley turned down out of safety concerns.[[9]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-9)

When the team travelled to [Pasadena, California](Pasadena%2C_California "Pasadena, California") to play in the [1934 Rose Bowl](1934_Rose_Bowl "1934 Rose Bowl") against [Stanford](Stanford_University "Stanford University"), however, it was determined by Crowley's successor [Lou Little](Lou_Little "Lou Little") that the team required a live mascot for the occasion, though he was unable to find any lions available to rent in the region prior to their departure. An alumnus who lived in [Tucson](Tucson%2C_Arizona "Tucson, Arizona") had offered a wild Mexican boar to the university, which Little vetoed.[[10]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-10) Luckily, upon the team's arrival the day before the game, they were greeted by alumnus [Herman J. Mankiewicz](Herman_J._Mankiewicz "Herman J. Mankiewicz") with a lion on a leash. Little accepted, and Columbia would go on to win the game.[[11]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-11)[[12]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-12) In 1963, four students rented a 300-pound lion named Simba for a day from a theatrical rental agency in Manhattan to use in a game against [Princeton](Princeton_University "Princeton University"). It was kept in a cage under the scoreboard.[[13]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-13)

### Later history

Multiple statues of the Columbia Lion have been commissioned and placed around Columbia's campus. A sculpture of a lion by [Frederick Roth](Frederick_Roth "Frederick Roth"), donated by the Class of 1899, was placed at [Baker Field](Robert_K._Kraft_Field_at_Lawrence_A._Wien_Stadium "Robert K. Kraft Field at Lawrence A. Wien Stadium") to commemorate its opening in 1924.[[14]](Roar-ee_t

Based on my research, here's the information about the University of Pennsylvania's official mascot:

## Official Mascot: **The Quaker**

**Key Details:**

- **Nickname:** Penn Quakers (or simply "Quakers")
- **Alternative Name:** "The Red and the Blue" (referring to school colors)
- **School Colors:** Red and Blue
- **Connection:** The mascot honors the university's founder, Benjamin Franklin, and Pennsylvania's colonial history with William Penn, a member of the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers)

**Additional Context:**
- The Penn Quakers are the athletic teams of the University of Pennsylvania
- The university sponsors 33 varsity sports
- They compete in the Ivy League (primary conference) and NCAA Division I FCS
- Their home stadium is Franklin Field in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

Unlike some universities that have specific costumed mascot characters with individual names (like "Touchdown" the bear at Cornell or "Rhett" the Boston Terrier at Boston University), Penn's mascot is simply referred to as "The Quaker" — a reference to the historical and cultural significance of Quakers in Pennsylvania's founding. The mascot appears in imagery and on athletics logos, representing the school's heritage and identity.

**Keggy the Keg** is the unofficial mascot of [Dartmouth College](Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College"), an [Ivy League](Ivy_League "Ivy League") college in [Hanover, New Hampshire](Hanover%2C_New_Hampshire "Hanover, New Hampshire"), United States. Keggy is an [anthropomorphic](Anthropomorphic "Anthropomorphic") [beer keg](Keg "Keg"), created in 2003 by members of the college humor magazine the *[Dartmouth Jack-O-Lantern](Dartmouth_Jack-O-Lantern "Dartmouth Jack-O-Lantern")*, to fill the mascot void that followed the abolition of the unofficial [Native American mascot](Native_American_mascot_controversy "Native American mascot controversy") in 1974.[[1]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-1) Due to its nature, the mascot was controversial on Dartmouth's campus, and it was reported on in a variety of national media. With time, however, it has become an "ingrained part of Dartmouth culture".[[2]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-TheD-Stuart-2)

## Context and creation

After dropping the mascot of the [Indian](Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas"), Dartmouth had no official mascot.[[3]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-3) Dartmouth continued to be known by its nickname of "The Big Green," but, citing the ambiguity, lack of dynamism, and intangibility of having no mascot, the Dartmouth Student Assembly proposed a student poll in spring 2003 to decide upon a new mascot. While the Moose came in first in this poll,[[4]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-4) many students remained dissatisfied with the choice, and the moose lost a final poll to "no mascot." Chris Plehal and Nic Duquette, students at the *[Jack-O-Lantern](Dartmouth_Jack-O-Lantern "Dartmouth Jack-O-Lantern")* humor magazine, expressed interest in creating a mascot that "wasn't racist, biased or sexist, yet [was] entirely unacceptable."[[5]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-d-orbuch-5) In an effort to force the administration to adopt a more interesting mascot, they created Keggy, an anthropomorphic keg that represents "the most obvious Dartmouth stereotype: the beer-swilling *[Animal House](National_Lampoon's_Animal_House "National Lampoon's Animal House")* fraternity culture."[[6]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-6)

## Reactions

Reaction to Keggy's introduction was mixed: the student body president personally endorsed Keggy in the mascot search,[[7]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-d-garland-7) while the College newspaper *[The Dartmouth](The_Dartmouth "The Dartmouth")* reported a mixed student reaction and published opposing opinions.[[5]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-d-orbuch-5)[[8]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-8)[[9]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-9)[[10]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-10) The paper also reported on "flak" over the mascot from College administrators,[[7]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-d-garland-7) though the Dean of the College lauded the students' capacity to "come up with imaginativ

**Touchdown**, or the *[Big Red](Cornell_Big_Red "Cornell Big Red") Bear*, is the unofficial mascot of [Cornell University](Cornell_University "Cornell University"). The first mascot was a black bear introduced in 1915 by the Cornell University Athletic Association. Three more live bears over the course of approximately two decades also made appearances at Cornell until the live bear was replaced by costumed students some years later. Touchdown appears on the logo for [Cornell Athletics](Cornell_Big_Red "Cornell Big Red"), and is represented in a statue erected outside Teagle Hall in 2015.

## History

### Touchdown I

The first mascot at Cornell was a black bear that the Cornell University Athletic Association (CUAA) acquired in the fall of 1915. The CUAA spent twenty-five dollars, excluding shipping costs, raised by the revenue from season ticket sales to purchase the bear. The bear was purchased after the manager of the football team received a letter from an animal trainer in [Old Town, Maine](Old_Town%2C_Maine "Old Town, Maine"). This year also marked the first year Cornell football went undefeated, which led to fans believing that Touchdown was a good omen.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1)

Touchdown appeared at all of the games played by the Cornell football team that year. At the games, Touchdown was tethered to a stepladder so that he could climb on the home sideline of the field. He also climbed a goal post before each game, which quickly became a tradition for the fans.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 38

At the [Harvard](Harvard_Crimson "Harvard Crimson") game of 1915, Touchdown traveled with the team to [Cambridge, Massachusetts](Cambridge%2C_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"). The night before the game, Touchdown was sleeping in a cage in the lobby of the Lenox Hotel, per request of the manager of the hotel. At four o'clock in the morning of the game, several Harvard students stole Touchdown by posing as caretakers of the bear giving Touchdown a routine morning walk.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1) Touchdown was found later that morning by Cornell's trainer who heard cries coming from Harvard's baseball cage. Touchdown was only retrieved, however, after a posse of Cornell athletic managers stole the keys to the cage from a Harvard janitor who refused to open it without orders from Harvard football manager.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1) The janitor was reprimanded by being locked in an office.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1) Later that day at the game, the Cornell football team defeated the Crimson, ending Harvard's thirty-game winning streak in football.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1)

**Roar-ee the Lion** is the current incarnation of the **Columbia Lion**, the official mascot of [Columbia University](Columbia_University "Columbia University") and the [Columbia Lions](Columbia_Lions "Columbia Lions"). Already a long established symbol of the university, it was first adopted as the university's mascot in 1910 under the name "Leo Columbiae", and was renamed Roar-ee the Lion in 2005. Throughout its history, the Lion has been represented by live specimens on several occasions, including the [1934 Rose Bowl](1934_Rose_Bowl "1934 Rose Bowl") and a 1963 football game against [Princeton](Princeton_University "Princeton University"). During the early 20th century, Matilda the Harlem Goat was an unofficial mascot for the university. [Barnard College](Barnard_College "Barnard College") possesses its own mascot, the Barnard Bear.

## History

### Proposal and adoption

The idea of having a lion as the mascot of Columbia was first proposed by George Brokaw Compton at the April 5, 1910 meeting of the alumni association. The lion had been a longstanding unofficial symbol of the university, having frequently been used as a design motif on the university's campus even before its adoption. It was possibly derived from the coat of arms of King [George II](George_II_of_Great_Britain "George II of Great Britain"), under whom the school was founded in 1754.[[1]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-1)[[2]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-:2-2)

Its adoption was not uncontroversial, however. As the Lion, which was named "Leo Columbiae", was chosen in connection with Columbia's other royal imagery, a product of [Columbia's colonial past](Colonial_colleges "Colonial colleges"), some considered it a sign of excessive conservatism and a symbol of "servility to British Royalty".[[3]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-3) The Eagle was floated as an alternative, in line with the university's patriotic renaming following American independence: "For Kings College, the Lion, but the Eagle for [Columbia](Columbia_(personification) "Columbia (personification)")".[[4]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-4) The Goat, specifically Matilda the Harlem Goat, was also proposed, allegedly as a joke.[[5]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-5) Nevertheless, Leo was approved by the Student Board on May 4, 1910.[[2]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-:2-2)[[6]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-6)

### Live mascots

The first live Lion mascot used by the university football team was a [German Shepherd](German_Shepherd "German Shepherd") named Chief, who was presented to the team in 1925 and used for a short period of time.[[7]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-7) On October 24, 1928, a freshman suggested in the *[Columbia Daily Spectator](Columbia_Daily_Spectator "Columbia Daily Spectator")* that the university acquire an actual lion to use at football games, claiming that lions "are not very expensive at wild animal dealers," and "would grow up well tamed, meek and mild" if purchased as cubs.[[8]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-8) Several days later, an alumnus offered to donate a live lion cub to the university to serve as its mascot, which football Coach Charley Crowley turned down out of safety concerns.[[9]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-9)

When the team travelled to [Pasadena, California](Pasadena%2C_California "Pasadena, California") to play in the [1934 Rose Bowl](1934_Rose_Bowl "1934 Rose Bowl") against [Stanford](Stanford_University "Stanford University"), however, it was determined by Crowley's successor [Lou Little](Lou_Little "Lou Little") that the team required a live mascot for the occasion, though he was unable to find any lions available to rent in the region prior to their departure. An alumnus who lived in [Tucson](Tucson%2C_Arizona "Tucson, Arizona") had offered a wild Mexican boar to the university, which Little vetoed.[[10]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-10) Luckily, upon the team's arrival the day before the game, they were greeted by alumnus [Herman J. Mankiewicz](Herman_J._Mankiewicz "Herman J. Mankiewicz") with a lion on a leash. Little accepted, and Columbia would go on to win the game.[[11]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-11)[[12]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-12) In 1963, four students rented a 300-pound lion named Simba for a day from a theatrical rental agency in Manhattan to use in a game against [Princeton](Princeton_University "Princeton University"). It was kept in a cage under the scoreboard.[[13]](Roar-ee_the_Lion#cite_note-13)

**Keggy the Keg** is the unofficial mascot of [Dartmouth College](Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College"), an [Ivy League](Ivy_League "Ivy League") college in [Hanover, New Hampshire](Hanover%2C_New_Hampshire "Hanover, New Hampshire"), United States. Keggy is an [anthropomorphic](Anthropomorphic "Anthropomorphic") [beer keg](Keg "Keg"), created in 2003 by members of the college humor magazine the *[Dartmouth Jack-O-Lantern](Dartmouth_Jack-O-Lantern "Dartmouth Jack-O-Lantern")*, to fill the mascot void that followed the abolition of the unofficial [Native American mascot](Native_American_mascot_controversy "Native American mascot controversy") in 1974.[[1]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-1) Due to its nature, the mascot was controversial on Dartmouth's campus, and it was reported on in a variety of national media. With time, however, it has become an "ingrained part of Dartmouth culture".[[2]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-TheD-Stuart-2)

## Context and creation

After dropping the mascot of the [Indian](Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas"), Dartmouth had no official mascot.[[3]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-3) Dartmouth continued to be known by its nickname of "The Big Green," but, citing the ambiguity, lack of dynamism, and intangibility of having no mascot, the Dartmouth Student Assembly proposed a student poll in spring 2003 to decide upon a new mascot. While the Moose came in first in this poll,[[4]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-4) many students remained dissatisfied with the choice, and the moose lost a final poll to "no mascot." Chris Plehal and Nic Duquette, students at the *[Jack-O-Lantern](Dartmouth_Jack-O-Lantern "Dartmouth Jack-O-Lantern")* humor magazine, expressed interest in creating a mascot that "wasn't racist, biased or sexist, yet [was] entirely unacceptable."[[5]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-d-orbuch-5) In an effort to force the administration to adopt a more interesting mascot, they created Keggy, an anthropomorphic keg that represents "the most obvious Dartmouth stereotype: the beer-swilling *[Animal House](National_Lampoon's_Animal_House "National Lampoon's Animal House")* fraternity culture."[[6]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-6)

## Reactions

Reaction to Keggy's introduction was mixed: the student body president personally endorsed Keggy in the mascot search,[[7]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-d-garland-7) while the College newspaper *[The Dartmouth](The_Dartmouth "The Dartmouth")* reported a mixed student reaction and published opposing opinions.[[5]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-d-orbuch-5)[[8]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-8)[[9]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-9)[[10]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-10) The paper also reported on "flak" over the mascot from College administrators,[[7]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-d-garland-7) though the Dean of the College lauded the students' capacity to "come up with imaginative and creative ideas."[[5]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-d-orbuch-5)

Keggy subsequently received media attention beyond the College at other Ivy League newspapers and on several national media outlets.[[11]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-11)[[12]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-12) [Michael Wilbon](Michael_Wilbon "Michael Wilbon") of <ESPN>'s *[Pardon the Interruption](Pardon_the_Interruption "Pardon the Interruption")* called Keggy "some stupid beer thing,"[[13]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-13) and *<Playboy>* magazine published a feature on Keggy as part of a "Mascots Talk Back" series.[[14]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-14) A posting of a photo of Keggy on <CollegeHumor> was popular enough to receive status as a National Pick.[[15]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-15)[[16]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-16) In August, 2012 Yahoo Sports ranked Keggy the Keg as the #1 Most Unique Mascot.[[17]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-17)

## History

Shortly after Keggy's introduction in 2003, a group of students stole the Keggy costume from its home in the [Sigma Nu](Sigma_Nu "Sigma Nu") fraternity library and sent threatening notes to Keggy's creators, including photographs of the mascot bound and gagged with one black eye.[[18]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-18) Some thought this to be a publicity stunt by the creators, but the mascot had truly been stolen. Keggy was eventually returned with minor damage to the costume.[[19]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-19)

Keggy continued to make occasional appearances at Dartmouth sporting events, and became an "ingrained part of Dartmouth culture":[[2]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-TheD-Stuart-2) at Dartmouth's 2005 Winter Carnival celebration, students named the snow sculpture of a large ship "Captain Keggy's Carnival Cruiser."[[20]](Keggy_the_Keg#cite_note-20) In early 2006, College officials denied Keggy entrance to a sold-out hockey game (officials cited fire code concerns with the capacity crowd), prompting a *Jack-O-Lantern*-penned editorial in *[The Dartmouth](The_Dartmouth "The Dartmouth

**Nickname:** Big Green

**Mascot - "Keggy the Keg":**
- **Keggy the Keg** is the unofficial mascot of Dartmouth College
- Keggy is an **anthropomorphic beer keg** - a costume that looks like a beer keg with arms, legs, and a face
- **Created in 2003** by members of the college humor magazine *The Dartmouth Jack-O-Lantern*
- **Purpose:** Created to fill the mascot void after the previous mascot (Native American "Indian") was dropped in 1974
- **Meaning:** Represents "the most obvious Dartmouth stereotype: the beer-swilling *Animal House* fraternity culture"

### Historical Context

After dropping the Native American mascot in 1974, Dartmouth had no official mascot for decades. Despite this, the college continued to be known by its nickname "The Big Green," with no mascot to accompany it. In 2003, the Dartmouth Student Assembly proposed a poll to decide on a new mascot (the Moose won the poll but lost a final vote to "no mascot"), prompting the creation of Keggy.

### Reception

- Keggy received mixed reactions initially but has since become an "ingrained part of Dartmouth culture"
- The mascot has received national media attention, including features on ESPN's *Pardon the Interruption*, *Playboy* magazine, and CollegeHumor
- In August 2012, Yahoo Sports ranked Keggy the Keg as the **#1 Most Unique Mascot**
- Despite some controversy and occasional conflicts with college administration, Keggy continues to make appearances at Dartmouth sporting events and campus celebrations

The mascot remains unofficial, but it's widely recognized and beloved by the Dartmouth community as a fun, irreverent representation of campus culture.

**Touchdown**, or the *[Big Red](Cornell_Big_Red "Cornell Big Red") Bear*, is the unofficial mascot of [Cornell University](Cornell_University "Cornell University"). The first mascot was a black bear introduced in 1915 by the Cornell University Athletic Association. Three more live bears over the course of approximately two decades also made appearances at Cornell until the live bear was replaced by costumed students some years later. Touchdown appears on the logo for [Cornell Athletics](Cornell_Big_Red "Cornell Big Red"), and is represented in a statue erected outside Teagle Hall in 2015.

## History

### Touchdown I

The first mascot at Cornell was a black bear that the Cornell University Athletic Association (CUAA) acquired in the fall of 1915. The CUAA spent twenty-five dollars, excluding shipping costs, raised by the revenue from season ticket sales to purchase the bear. The bear was purchased after the manager of the football team received a letter from an animal trainer in [Old Town, Maine](Old_Town%2C_Maine "Old Town, Maine"). This year also marked the first year Cornell football went undefeated, which led to fans believing that Touchdown was a good omen.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1)

Touchdown appeared at all of the games played by the Cornell football team that year. At the games, Touchdown was tethered to a stepladder so that he could climb on the home sideline of the field. He also climbed a goal post before each game, which quickly became a tradition for the fans.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 38

At the [Harvard](Harvard_Crimson "Harvard Crimson") game of 1915, Touchdown traveled with the team to [Cambridge, Massachusetts](Cambridge%2C_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"). The night before the game, Touchdown was sleeping in a cage in the lobby of the Lenox Hotel, per request of the manager of the hotel. At four o'clock in the morning of the game, several Harvard students stole Touchdown by posing as caretakers of the bear giving Touchdown a routine morning walk.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1) Touchdown was found later that morning by Cornell's trainer who heard cries coming from Harvard's baseball cage. Touchdown was only retrieved, however, after a posse of Cornell athletic managers stole the keys to the cage from a Harvard janitor who refused to open it without orders from Harvard football manager.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1) The janitor was reprimanded by being locked in an office.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1) Later that day at the game, the Cornell football team defeated the Crimson, ending Harvard's thirty-game winning streak in football.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1)

The next week, the football team took a trip to [Atlantic City](Atlantic_City "Atlantic City") before the big <Thanksgiving> game against the [University of Pennsylvania](University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania"). At this point in the season, Touchdown had begun go into hibernation and was less vivacious than he was earlier in the season.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1) When Touchdown was woken to pose for pictures with the football team on a boardwalk at Atlantic City, he instead ran into the nearest door open. After running wild in a taffy shop, Touchdown escaped down a pier and jumped into the ocean.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1) Two football players, Booty Hunkin and Walt Lalley, used a life raft with no paddles to rescue Touchdown who was unable to swim. Touchdown walked back to the hotel alone.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1)

Touchdown was deeper into the beginning stages of hibernation at the Thanksgiving Day football game. UPenn had brought either a [coyote](Coyote "Coyote") or a [husky](Alaskan_Husky "Alaskan Husky") to the game, and walked it over to meet Touchdown right before the game started.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1) When Penn's mascot came close enough, Touchdown smacked it across the face and knocked it out.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1) Cornell went on to defeat Penn 24-9 during the game.

After the season was over, the football team had to make a decision about the fate of Touchdown. Although there was some talk about sending him to a zoo in Rome, the bear was eventually sent back to Old Town, Maine, where he lived the rest of his life.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1)

### Touchdown II

In 1916, Walt Lalley, now the team's manager, recruited a black bear cub from Maine to take the place of Touchdown I.[[2]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-2) Although Touchdown II represented Cornell on the sidelines for the latter part of the season, he was kept under close protection off the field to prevent another kidnapping attempt.[[3]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-3)

On the final game of the season, the students of University of Pennsylvania brought a bear of their own onto the sideline named "Jack Victory," who, along with the football team, stole the show from Touchdown and the Big Red, defeating Cornell 23–0. The Cornell team then abandoned Touchdown II on the field after the loss. He was then briefly adopted by Penn, and accompanied Penn's bear and the team to their [Rose Bowl](Rose_Bowl_Game "Rose Bowl Game") match against the [Oregon Ducks](Oregon_Ducks "Oregon Ducks").[[4]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-4) The bear's whereabouts after trip are unknown.

### Touchdown III

Due to [World War I](World_War_I "World War I") capturing the attention of Cornell's students and faculty, there was no mascot for the 1917 and 1918 football seasons.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 37 Once campus life returned to normal in 1919, Montana-based Cornell alumnus R. H. Barney '17 donated a local bear for use as the football team's mascot. Dubbed Touchdown III, the bear's arrival at Cornell was notable enough to receive mention in the [New York Times](New_York_Times "New York Times").[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 38

The Cornell community's reception of Touchdown III was generally positive, although the mascot had powerful enemies. The *[Cornell Daily Sun](Cornell_Daily_Sun "Cornell Daily Sun")* reported that Touchdown III was "the admiration of the entire [football] squad, as well as the coaching staff," echoing the Ithaca community's general sentiment.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 39 However, Cornell University Athletic Association head [Romeyn Berry](Romeyn_Berry "Romeyn Berry") hated all bears, describing them as "disgusting . . . dangerous, ill-tempered, and unbelievably troublesome" and characterizing the original Touchdown as "hungry, mean, ill-bred, and dangerous." Thus, Berry was no fan of the new mascot.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 39

During the 1919 football season, Touchdown III was involved in a few minor events on Cornell's campus. The week after the season began, Touchdown III broke free from his living quarters on [Schoellkopf Field](Schoellkopf_Field "Schoellkopf Field"). Authorities and volunteers found the bear napping in a nearby grassy field, prompting a humorous *Sun* article entitled "Touchdown III Loses at Game of Hide and Seek."[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 40 Later on, Touchdown III led a parade of Cornell student demonstrators demanding higher salaries for professors. Touchdown III's involvement in this parade produced a classic photograph of the bear gnawing on a banner inscribed "I'm For Them Too."[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 41

Late in the season, the Cornell football team headed to New York City for a game against [Dartmouth College](Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College"). Although the team stayed at the [Hotel Pennsylvania](Hotel_Pennsylvania "Hotel Pennsylvania"), they rushed Touchdown III directly to the [Cornell Club](Cornell_Club "Cornell Club") on 44th Street, where a smoker for Cornell Alumni was taking place.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 41 This is the last known location of Touchdown III. Although legend states that he was sent to a zoo in [Akron, Ohio](Akron%2C_Ohio "Akron, Ohio"), Touchdown III's true fate is currently unknown.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 42

### The Bearless Years

After Touchdown III's departure in 1919, Cornell was left without a mascot for its football team. Cornell would not adopt a new mascot until 1939. This long period without a mascot can be at least partially attributed to bear-hating CUAA head [Romeyn Berry](Romeyn_Berry "Romeyn Berry"), whose tenure lasted until 1935.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 45 Some blame may also belong to [Gil Dobie](Gil_Dobie "Gil Dobie"), Cornell's football coach from 1920 to 1935, whose no-nonsense approach had little room for wildlife distractions.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 46

In fall of 1934, Cornell students decided to hold a pre-game party (or "Hop") before the Cornell vs. Dartmouth football game. At this Hop, Touchdown was revived as a life-sized painting. After Cornell won the football game, students attributed the victory to Touchdown's symbolic return.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 47

After Dartmouth, [University of Pennsylvania](University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania") was Cornell's next opponent. In an attempt to replicate the Dartmouth game's result, three Cornell undergrads drove to [Burnet Park](Burnet_Park "Burnet Park") Zoo in Syracuse and rented a bear as a temporary mascot. After the bear immediately destroyed the undergrads' trailer, Cornell students were forced to make do with [Romeyn Berry](Romeyn_Berry "Romeyn Berry") dressed in a fur coat as the mascot for the pre-game Penn rally.[[1]](Touchdown_(mascot)#cite_note-Foote-1): 48 However, the student movement to bring back a live bear mascot continued to gain steam
